In certain materials, the linear electro-optic (Pockels) effect allows direct control of the 10 refractive index with an applied electric field. In practice, material inhomogeneities and 11 defects cause the field inside the material to drift over macroscopic time scales. Such 12 phenomena degrade the reliability and stability of integrated electro-optic devices. Here, we 13 combine systematic measurements of dc electro-optic response, electronic transport, and 14 elemental composition to examine the microscopic origins of dc instability in nanofabricated 15 thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) devices. We identify two key sources of instability: the 16 metal-LN contact interface where Schottky barriers impede charge injection, and the oxide- 17 LN cladding interface where lithium diffusion occurs. Our work provides an electronic 18 understanding of a long-standing photonics issue, advancing a potential pathway toward 19 high-performance integrated electro-optic devices through materials-motivated design. 20

The ability to connect electronics and optics fundamentally underpins optical 21 communications and interconnects. Material phenomena that enable voltage-controlled optical 22 modulation form a broad class of electro-refractive and electro-absorptive effects, including the 23 Pockels, Franz-Keldysh, and free-carrier dispersion effects1. It therefore stands to reason that 24 electronic and photonic properties be considered together when designing such devices. This 25 approach has been implemented to great success in traditional semiconductor platforms such as 26 silicon and III-V semiconductors, achieving low drive voltages and ultra-compact footprints2–5. 27 However, for long-haul communications requiring low-loss and high-bandwidth operation, 28 Pockels electro-optic (EO) modulators based on wide-bandgap materials such as LN have long 29 been the preferred choice6. Because it is fundamentally rooted in the non-centrosymmetry of a 30 crystal, the Pockels EO effect stands out for its simplicity as a linear, non-absorptive refractive 31 index shift. Correspondingly, EO materials are generally understood not to suffer from many of 32 the material limitations intrinsic to other modulation schemes, such as free-carrier absorption7. 33 Such claims have been bolstered by rapid advances in high-performance and compact Pockels 34 modulators, largely driven by nanofabrication breakthroughs on the thin-film LN platform that 35 have enabled electrodes to be placed closer to the optical waveguide, resulting in efficient overlap 36 between the electric and optical fields8,9. The regime of strong EO has also made accessible new 37 functionalities, including low-power reconfigurable photonic circuits, broadband frequency 38 combs, ultrafast pulse generation and manipulation, and on-chip spectrometers10–14. Coupled with 39 the wafer-scale availability of TFLN, entire electro-optical systems can be miniaturized at scale 40 onto a wafer die using standard nanofabrication techniques14–16. 41

Many of the above-mentioned applications rely on the ability to control the operating point 42 of the EO device, which is ideally accomplished by applying bias dc fields. For this reason, it is 43 imperative that dc EO tuning is well-understood, especially as photonic systems grow more 44 complex and may no longer rely on power-hungry thermal tuning10,17. Ideally, the EO response 45 should quickly settle to a constant value after application of a step voltage input, as well as exhibit 46 high linearity with applied voltage (Fig. 1a,b). In practice, drift of the dc operating point degrades 47 the reliability of EO devices over time and the existence of a threshold in the EO response prevents 48 simple calibration of EO tuning, necessitating complex locking schemes18,19. In conventional LN 49 modulators based on low-confinement waveguides realized using proton exchange or Ti- 50 indiffusion, much research and development has been dedicated to bringing down drift rates to 51 feedback-acceptable levels20–23. However, thin-film structures have received limited attention as a 52 distinct format with its own set of material challenges, aggravated by the expanded role of surfaces 53


<!-- Page 5 -->


3

and interfaces24,25. Indeed, leakage current is relegated to a nonideality, rather than an appreciable 54 electronic response–an intrinsic consequence of charge carrier transport. 55

Here we show that the common simplification of TFLN as an ideal insulator during device 56 design limits the ability to engineer devices and systems with minimized EO instability. Like any 57 real crystal, TFLN has defects that can move, react, and trap charge carriers injected into the 58 material—effects intrinsically temporal in nature (Fig. 1c). No different from a semiconductor 59 device explicitly using free carriers, the electronic and optical responses of an EO device must be 60 designed for in tandem. We illustrate this by investigating the linearity and stability of the dc EO 61 response in congruent TFLN nanophotonic modulators at telecommunication wavelengths, in 62 response to a wide range of chemical and thermal processing conditions. Correlating device 63 performance changes with measurements of the material structure and electronic properties, we 64 develop a microscopic understanding of how the metal-LN contact interface influences thin-film 65 electro-optic response. Surprisingly, while the EO performance of a pristine and untreated TFLN 66 surface is highly sensitive to small variations in the nanofabrication process flow, we find that 67 plasma-induced damage arising during reactive ion etching can actually improve contact linearity, 68 simplifying the identification of different sources of dc drift throughout the entire device stack. 69 We therefore capitalize on this quasi-linear contact to quantitatively study charge-trapping 70 dynamics in oxide-cladded TFLN devices and investigate the influence of thermal annealing. 71 While annealing is commonly used to improve device performance, we show such processing also 72 induces lithium diffusion at the oxide-LN cladding interface that contributes additional drift 73 pathways at long time scales (~hours). Beyond identifying specific electronic interfaces for 74 targeted electro-optic engineering, these results present practical advancements in TFLN device 75 physics that can be immediately applied to the study of other electrically-coupled device 76 phenomena such as ferroelectric domain inversion and electro-acoustics25–27. 77

Experimental details 78

We start by examining air-cladded devices fabricated using standard nanofabrication 79 processes for x-cut TFLN modulators (Fig. 1d, inset). Briefly, after patterning waveguides with 80 electron-beam lithography and Ar-ion etching, redeposited material and residual resist arising from 81 the dry etch process are removed with a series of wet chemical cleans (see Methods for details). 82 Devices are then annealed in an oxygen environment at 520 ºC, which has been shown to reduce 83 optical loss and photorefractive contributions associated with damage from ion slicing used to 84 realize TFLN, as well as electron beam irradiation28–31. Photolithography, Ti/Au evaporation, and 85 lift-off are then used to define contacts to TFLN. 86

The time-domain response is characterized using a variant of so-called phase-tracking 87 measurements23, wherein we monitor the optical mode splitting of a double ring device as a 88 function of time after a step voltage is applied (Fig. 1d). We define the temporal EO response as 89 the change in optical mode splitting, normalized to the applied voltage. Coupled ring devices are 90 both technologically relevant for emerging photonic devices such as microwave-to-optical 91 transducers and frequency-domain beamsplitters and isolators32–35, as well as useful sensors of the 92 internal electric field distribution. Importantly, these measurements can be conducted in an 93 ambient environment: monitoring the splitting is a differential measurement that is first-order 94 insensitive to common-mode noise (e.g. thermal shifts from either the room temperature or 95 changes in the light in-coupling efficiency). Unless otherwise specified, the applied voltage for 96 these measurements is 30 V. The EO voltage dependence is measured with the same experimental 97

setup using a staircase waveform interleaved with periods of 0 V to discharge the device and more 98 accurately capture the step response (Supplementary Fig. 1). This measurement is performed prior 99 to any long-term dc drift measurement to avoid hysteresis36,37. 100

Influence of the contact interface on short-term dc drift and linearity 101

For devices following the baseline fabrication flow without any intentional contact 102 treatment, the step response is marked by a rapid initial transient that overshoots and then settles 103 into the long-term drift response over the course of <10 minutes (Fig. 1e, inset). Additionally, for 104 some dies the EO response shows negligible voltage dependence before surpassing a threshold 105 voltage, at which point the resonance shift rapidly increases in magnitude (Baseline 2, Fig. 1f). 106 Both fast transients and thresholding mark significant departures from the ideal response and may 107 render dc EO biasing unreliable in practical applications. Interestingly, we observe both linear and 108 nonlinear EO responses across several dies following nominally identical fabrication flows, 109 although initial transients are common regardless of the presence or absence of a voltage threshold. 110 This variability suggests the pristine TFLN contact chemistry is readily altered by nanofabrication 111 processes, including those commonly considered benign such as organic residue cleans. We are 112 unsure of the exact origin of these variations but surmise they could be due to fluctuations in the 113 concentration and temperature of the wet chemical cleans at the time of sample processing, leading 114 to different levels of remaining redeposition. Indeed, x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) of 115 TFLN taken after wet cleaning indicates that the balance of Li, Nb, and O at the surface is highly 116 sensitive to each of the chemicals employed (Supplementary Fig. 2). 117

To this end, one approach to combat device variability is to enforce contact linearity with 118 a deliberate surface treatment prior to metal deposition. Our technique is based on etching so that 119 any surface contaminants are simultaneously removed while modifying the TFLN surface states 120 (Fig. 2a). Both a pure Ar and a F-based (Ar + C3F8) plasma were investigated for this step, as these 121 gas chemistries are commonly used in nanofabrication and have been observed to influence low- 122 frequency roll-off of the EO response24. In contrast to the baseline samples, we find that both the 123 Ar and F-based plasma etched contacts suppress initial transients and maintain linearity in their 124 voltage response (Fig. 2b,c). This occurs despite ion-induced damage expected from the physical 125 etching component, evident in XPS of etched samples showing significantly broadened Nb 4s and 126 Li 1s peaks (Supplementary Fig. 2). Although the behavior at short time scales is qualitatively 127 similar for Ar and F-based plasma, the long-term dc drift behavior is much richer for the F-exposed 128 sample, displaying multiple enhancements and decays of the EO response compared to the 129 monotonic decay of the pure Ar etch. This might be attributed to the specific chemical reactions 130 associated with the F-containing etch, which can deposit undesired dielectric layers that provide 131 further avenues for charge redistribution38. Specifically, F can react with Li and other etching 132 byproducts to produce nonvolatile fluorinated compounds such as LiFx salts or fluoropolymers, as 133 indicated by XPS (Supplementary Fig. 2). 134

Electronic mechanism of the plasma-etched contact 135

To delve further into the underlying mechanism of the different contacts, we also compared 136 the EO voltage response to the electronic characteristics of the device stack, measured using simple 137 two-probe current-voltage measurements (Fig. 2,c-f). We observe a strong correspondence 138 between the leakage current and the EO response, indicating that electronic transport physics can 139 be used to interpret and predict EO performance. The threshold phenomenon can then be readily 140 explained as a consequence of rectifying contacts. This is clear from the I-V characteristic of the 141

Physically, this 147 reflects the charge carrier transmissivity across the potential barrier created between the metal and 148 LN. Because the current is clamped by the saturation current of the reverse-biased diode, in steady- 149 state most of the voltage drop occurs at the interface instead of the central region where the optical 150 mode resides (Fig. 3b). In EO devices, this manifests as an apparent lack of response when the 151 current saturates. However, at sufficiently high voltages the reverse-biased diode will break down 152 and start to conduct again due to barrier-lowering or tunneling processes induced by the steep band 153 bending at the interface39. Rapid initial transients therefore arise as a consequence of the step 154 voltage input when the conduction is contact-limited: the opposing contact diodes act to suppress 155 the voltage spike by rapidly increasing the reverse current, thereby clamping the overvoltage. The 156 excess carriers injected during breakdown then diffuse into the optical mode region and induce the 157 EO effect. We note this is a phenomenon distinct from simple displacement current contributions, 158 which occur on the timescale of the voltage supply ramp time (~s). Interestingly, while diffusion 159 can be slow in a polar oxide, the relevant carrier lifetimes (~μs) are orders of magnitude shorter 160 than what we typically observe (~minutes)40,41. This discrepancy necessitates further intensive 161 study of diffusion processes in congruent TFLN at room temperature. One possibility is the abrupt 162 hot injection of charges induces local heating that adds additional index shifts through the thermo- 163 optic and pyroelectric effect before thermalizing42. 164

The plasma-treated samples can similarly be interpreted as engineering an electronic 165 contact to quickly transition from rectifying to transmitting I-V, therefore appearing quasi-linear 166 (Fig. 2c,d). The specific mechanism by which the potential barrier is modified depends on the 167 charge carrier involved. As a polar oxide, the mobility of charge conduction in LN lies intermediate 168 between band conduction in crystalline semiconductors and hopping conduction in amorphous 169 solids. Because of strong electrostatic interactions with the lattice, electrons in such materials self- 170 localize to a single lattice site, forming small polarons43. Electron transport in LN is thus typically 171 interpreted in terms of polaron motion, encompassing bound polarons trapped at niobium antisites 172 (NbLi) and free polarons hopping between reduced niobium sites40,43–45. Although ionic motion can 173 also contribute to charge transport, all measurements were taken at room temperature, far below 174 the transition temperatures required to thermally activate ions as indicated by Arrhenius studies of 175 conductivity45. 176

The mechanism of the plasma-treated contact is then readily elucidated from XPS of the 177 Nb 3d peak, showing clear emergence of the reduced Nb4+ and Nb3+ valence states at the surface 178 after etching (Fig. 3c,d). Surface reduction of metal oxides after Ar sputtering in vacuum is 179 commonly observed and generally attributed to preferential sputtering of oxygen atoms46, which 180 can occur even with low energy (<1 keV) ion milling (Supplementary Fig. 3). In LN, this may be 181 further compounded by loss of Li, leaving behind Li vacancy defects that Nb atoms can 182 subsequently fill43. Consequently, because both NbLi and reduced Nb serve as hopping sites for 183 different species of polaron, chemical reduction effectively modifies the local conductivity of the 184

6

LN in contact with the electrode. Importantly, due to the complex interplay between different 185 hopping conduction mechanisms and their associated mobilities, LN conductivity does not in 186 general increase monotonically with degree of reduction and greatly depends on the specific defect 187 reactions incurred44. Although a clear deficiency of oxygen is detected in XPS post-etch (Fig. 3e,f), 188 it is difficult to quantitatively analyze Li vacancy formation due to the emergence of the damage 189 peak near Li 1s line, and therefore the relative contributions of bound and free polaron hopping 190 (Supplementary Fig. 2). However, a simple I-V comparison between a pristine and blanket-etched 191 TFLN sample suggests that for our system the contact resistance should decrease (Supplementary 192 Fig. 4). Such plasma etches have also been used to create ohmic contacts in ultra-wide bandgap 193 semiconductors, ostensibly due to the high-density formation of donor-acting oxygen vacancies47. 194 In this view, the targeted surface reduction at the contact acts as a form of chemical doping for 195 polar oxides in analogy to traditional impurity doping in semiconductors, effectively thinning the 196 barrier or otherwise mediating the removal of dangling bonds and other trap states at the 197 interface48. 198

Influence of thermal annealing on long-term dc drift 199

DC stability is expected to be sensitive not only to local chemical modifications, but also 200 to the presence of defects and impurities throughout the entire material stack. These 201 inhomogeneities may trap (or detrap) charge carriers, or may be physically redistributed to screen 202 the applied field. In this view each independent drift process can be associated with a lifetime ߬௜, 203 and arises in the dc drift curve as a linear combination of N exponential decays: 204

ܧܱ(ݐ) = ∑ ܿ௜݁−௧/ఛ೔ ே ௜=1 + ܧ𝑂𝑂∞ (2). 205

The coefficients ܿ௜ are weighting factors that can be positive or negative, and whose magnitude 206 can be associated with the initial concentration of the participating defect or impurity49.  ܧ𝑂𝑂∞ is 207 the steady-state EO response after all the decays saturate. Such a model has also been understood 208 from an RC-ladder network perspective, in which each RC block captures electronic 209 inhomogeneity arising from interfaces or anisotropy23 (Supplementary Fig. 5). In practical devices, 210 the exact distribution of defects and impurities is modified by thermal cycling, e.g. from annealing 211 steps used to repair lattice damage, sinter contacts, and passivate defects. By isolating the effect of 212 individual annealing steps on EO performance, we can probe material changes incurred by thermal 213 annealing after characteristic stages in TFLN fabrication (Fig. 4a). Specifically, in addition to post- 214 etch annealing which we term the “LN anneal,” we also investigated annealing after the deposition 215 of a SiO2 top-cladding, termed the “oxide anneal.” Such an anneal is typically justified as 216 improving the quality of oxide deposited by a low-temperature process such as plasma-enhanced 217 chemical vapor deposition (PECVD)22,29. Importantly, all device variations employ the Ar contact 218 etch to enforce quasi-linearity, enabling us to reliably probe the exponential decays of interest 219 without being obscured by the transient behavior of the contact (Supplementary Fig. 6). This need 220 is evident in the RC-ladder network picture, which assumes that the connection between the power 221 supply and the linear circuit modeling the trapping and screening processes is also linear, i.e. 222 capacitive or resistive (Supplementary Fig. 5). To this end, established defect spectroscopies such 223 as deep-level transient spectroscopy (DLTS) also require the development of an ohmic contact to 224 ensure the correct trap states are probed in the bulk instead of at the contact junctions50. 225

As a baseline, we consider a top-cladded device that has undergone no anneals. The lack 226 of annealing unveils a fast rise time (߬1 = 7(1) × 102 s) followed by a slow temporal decay of the 227

7

driving field, characterized by N=3 lifetimes total (Fig. 4b). This response is then compared to 228 devices that have undergone only the LN anneal, only the oxide anneal, or both. Although it is 229 difficult to identify the microscopic origin of every decay, we can use the phenomenological model 230 underlying Eq. 2 to infer material changes; the appearance or disappearance of a decay constant 231 should correspond with the appearance or disappearance of some dielectric inhomogeneity. 232 Characteristically, devices that have only undergone the LN anneal lose the fast initial rise and 233 exhibit dc drift well-fit by only N=2 lifetimes (Fig. 4c). In fact, the fast drift process (߬1 < 103 s) 234 vanishes with any combination of anneals (Fig. 4,c-e), indicating that annealing in general removes 235 a drift source intrinsic to nanofabricated TFLN-on-insulator. These initial defects may stem from 236 the ion-slicing process or initial etch, or from high energy electron irradiation during 237 lithography30,31.  Notably, any device that experiences an oxide anneal still requires at least N=3 238 lifetimes (Fig. 4d,e). This is observed even though the oxide anneal ostensibly repairs fast-drift 239 defects in the same manner as the LN anneal, implying that the presence of oxide during annealing 240 mediates the introduction of a different, unrelated relaxation pathway. 241

Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS) was used to obtain an understanding of the 242 specific structural changes incurred by the oxide anneal (Fig. 4f). Remarkably, samples that are 243 annealed in the presence of cladding oxide have a measurable and increased Li concentration at 244 the cladding-LN interface, indicating the decomposition of LN at the interface and subsequent Li 245 diffusion into the cladding51. Negligible change to the Li signal is observed in the buried oxide 246 layer, suggesting that the quality of the oxide also plays a role in the diffusion (see 247 Supplementary Fig. 7 for a comparison of the Li distribution in different cladding oxides). The 248 contributions to drift processes could be multifold; further study is required to identify if the 249 main temporal contribution stems from Li vacancies in the TFLN, Li ion contamination in the 250 cladding, or some combination of both. Li vacancies are associated with a variety of point 251 defects in LN, including NbLi defects serving as preferential trapping sites for bound polarons. 252 As such, an increased antisite concentration at the interface would certainly impact overall 253 charge carrier dynamics40,43. Preliminary scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) 254 imaging indicates that the LN is denser within 10-15 nm of the interface (Supplementary Fig. 8), 255 a signature of NbLi formation52. Alternatively, slow ion migration would result in an irreversible 256 screening process that could also help explain our observations of hysteresis, where the dc drift 257 after a long-term measurement is not reproducible and instead continues the decay of the 258 previous drift measurement (Supplementary Fig. 9). However, given that hysteresis occurs even 259 for samples that only experience the LN anneal (Fig. 4c), it is clear Li ion migration in the top 260 cladding can only partially explain memory effects. Other possible hysteretic contributions 261 inherent to the TFLN-on-insulator platform include ion migration in the TFLN or the buried 262 oxide, or ferroelectric domain inversion under the hot electrode22,36,37. 263

Conclusions 264

The effects of surface chemistry and interfaces on device performance in general, and on 265 reliable EO in particular, only become exacerbated as materials scale down in dimensions and 266 surface-volume ratios increase. We have developed an understanding of the interfacial conditions 267 that enable stable and linear EO operation in TFLN nanophotonic devices. While thermal 268 annealing is generally assumed to improve device performance, here we show that TFLN electro- 269 optic devices must be carefully engineered to prevent concurrent Li diffusion into the cladding, in 270 the same way that silicon foundries are constrained by a thermal budget to prevent diffusion of 271 dopants. Moreover, small modifications to the contact interface drastically affect the evolution of 272


<!-- Page 10 -->


8

dc response, highlighting the need to fully understand the electronic properties of TFLN beyond 273 an ideal defect-free dielectric to fully realize its potential in electro-optic devices. To this end, we 274 exploited the polaronic nature of conduction in LN to develop a chemical reduction protocol that 275 extends contact linearity, despite etch damage. Contact engineering is well-understood in 276 integrated circuits and silicon photonics, but uncommonly used in electro-optic devices that do not 277 explicitly rely on carrier injection for index modulation. The utility of linear contacts for efficient 278 and stable dc EO coupling is simple and can be generalized to other EO platforms such as polymer 279 modulators, barium titanate, and lithium tantalate53–55. Although the devices we present still 280 require a low-frequency feedback control loop to lock bias points, free-running operation and 281 therefore greater system complexity should be possible with device processing advances informed 282 by the material understanding we have obtained. 283
